chief_complaint: annular scaly red patch with active scaling border
hpi_details: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with annular scaly red patch with active scaling border. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks the spreading red ring on his skin is a tick bite from a recent camping trip or an allergic reaction to a gym mat.
concerns: He is worried that it might be Lyme disease from a tick bite and could cause chronic joint pain that stops him from working out.
expectations: He hopes to get tested for Lyme disease and receive a prescription cream or antibiotic to clear the circular rash immediately.

investigation_events.title: KOH preparation of the active border
investigation_events.availability_message: The KOH preparation result is now available.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Tinea Corporis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Tinea Corporis: Topical Terbinafine cream BID for 2 weeks, avoid steroids, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Tinea Corporis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Nummular eczema without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rapidly spreading lesion with fever or systemic illness — consider deeper fungal infection or bacterial superinfection.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: annular scaly red patch with active scaling border

A 29-year-old male presents with a single annular, scaly, red patch with an actively scaling, expanding border that has been gradually worsening.
reference_soap.objective: Well-demarcated, annular erythematous plaque with a raised, scaling active border and mild central clearing. No satellite lesions, nail involvement, or systemic signs of infection noted.
reference_soap.plan: Plan for Tinea Corporis: Topical Terbinafine cream BID for 2 weeks, avoid steroids. Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Tinea Corporis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Tinea Corporis
Implement evidence-based management plan: Topical Terbinafine cream BID for 2 weeks, avoid steroids

teaching.one_liner: A dermatophyte fungal infection causing an expanding annular patch with an active scaling border.
red_flags: Rapidly spreading lesion with fever or systemic illness — consider deeper fungal infection or bacterial superinfection
Widespread or atypical lesions in an immunocompromised patient — risk of Majocchi granuloma or disseminated infection
No improvement (or worsening) after a full course of topical antifungal — reconsider the diagnosis before escalating treatment

must_ask.say: Does it have a scaling, active border?
How long has this been going on?
Any contact with gyms or animals?

history.answer: I noticed this red, scaly ring on my arm recently, and it has been spreading outward.
It started about two weeks ago as a small itchy red bump, and it has gradually enlarged into a ring.
It is just this single patch on the outer side of my right forearm. Nowhere else.
The edge is raised, bumpy, and flaky, while the very center looks clearer and flatter.
Yes, the circle has been slowly expanding outward over the past couple of weeks.
It is mildly itchy, especially when I get warm or sweat, but it does not really hurt or burn.
No, it stays there constantly once it appeared. It does not disappear and pop up elsewhere like hives.
No, I have never had a skin lesion or rash like this before.
I haven't had any fever, chills, or body aches, though I have been feeling a bit run-down and fatigued lately.
No, my mouth, lips, eyes, and private areas are completely normal without any sores.
No, the skin is not blistering, peeling off, or bruising. It just has dry flakes along the rim.
No, my breathing is completely fine, and I have had no facial swelling or dizziness.
No, I haven't started any new prescription drugs, antibiotics, or pain medications.
No, I haven't switched soaps, detergents, cosmetics, or worn new jewelry.
I work out regularly at a public fitness center and share the weight benches, and my roommate recently brought home an adopted kitten.
No one in my house has a rash like this right now, although the kitten has had a couple of patchy spots.
No recent hiking, camping, tick bites, or travel out of town.
I put a little bit of moisturizing lotion on it, but I haven't used any medicated creams or steroid ointments.
No, I have never had eczema, asthma, or hay fever.
No joint aches, swelling, or changes in my fingernails.
I am in a monogamous relationship, and neither of us has had any genital sores or unusual rashes.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes or high blood pressure.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamins.
I don't have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or materials.
I do not smoke cigarettes or use any nicotine products.
I drink one or two beers occasionally on the weekend with friends.
I work in an office at an IT firm and live in an apartment with a roommate.
No one in my family has chronic skin diseases like psoriasis or severe allergies.
I thought it might be a tick bite from a camping trip I took last weekend, or maybe some skin reaction from the wrestling mats at the gym.
I'm really worried this could be Lyme disease from a tick and that it'll mess up my joints and leave me exhausted for months.
I'm hoping to get tested for Lyme disease and leave with a prescription cream or pills to wipe out this red ring.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, comfortable young man in no acute distress.
Well-demarcated, 4-centimeter annular erythematous plaque with a raised, actively scaling red border and mild central clearing on the forearm; no satellite pustules or skin denudation.
Oral mucosa is pink and hydrated without erythema, erosions, vesicles, or white plaques.
Conjunctivae are normal without hyperemia, discharge, or pseudomembranes; sclerae are non-icteric.
No palpable cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Fingernails and toenails are smooth and intact without pitting, subungual hyperkeratosis, or onycholysis; no joint swelling or tenderness.
No erythematous papules, ulcers, or scaling lesions on the external genitalia or groins.
